title: The Knot That Cannot Be Untied: Lewisham, Los Alamos, Harwell, and the Shape Named After Him
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Lewisham, birth in a bank clerk's house
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia, 'Tony Skyrme', gives 5 December 1922. Coordinate corrected from the gathering pass, whose 51.4452, -0.0209 fell about 2.1 km south in the Catford area; Nominatim gives 51.4624, -0.0102 for Lewisham.
stops.campa: Tony Hilton Royle Skyrme is born on the fifth of December 1922 in Lewisham, south London, the son of a bank clerk. The borough is terraces and commuter trains, a place that makes clerks and expects to keep them. No plaque will ever mark the house. The name he carries out of it attaches to no address at all, but to a shape: a knot of field lines called the skyrmion, present wherever a proton is and nowhere in particular. Lewisham keeps nothing of him.
suggested_refs: The birth registration for Lewisham, December quarter 1922

stops.name: Lewisham, the tide machine in his grandfather's house
stops.date_confidence: undated. Wikipedia records a boarding school in Lewisham but gives no year for it, and Skyrme's own account places the tide machine only somewhere in childhood. 1930 is a placeholder for the school years, not a claim. The gathering pass asserted 1930 as attested; it is not.
stops.campa: In his grandfather's house stands a Thomson-Doodson-Legé tide-predicting machine, a cabinet of brass gears and pulleys that turns the pull of the moon into a drawn curve of tides. The boy watches it work. He is at a boarding school in Lewisham in these years; no source gives the year, and nothing else of his childhood mind survives. What survives is the machine and his own account of it four decades later. William Thomson, Lord Kelvin, designed the first of that line, and Skyrme will quote Kelvin at the end of his life.
stops.quote: The ingenuity of its mechanism, whereby it could produce this complicated pattern of tides, had considerable influence on me.
stops.quote_source: T.H.R. Skyrme, Cosener's House talk (1984), published as 'The Origins of Skyrmions' in A Breadth of Physics: Proc. Peierls 80th Birthday Symposium (World Scientific, 1988), pp.193-202; quoted in Ian J.R. Aitchison, arXiv:2001.09944, p.5
suggested_refs: Surviving Thomson-Doodson-Legé tide-predicting machines; the Kelvin tidal analyser lineage
sources: Ian J.R. Aitchison, 'Tony Skyrme and the Origins of Skyrmions', arXiv:2001.09944 (2020), p.5

stops.name: Eton College, the scholarship
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No source consulted gives the year of entry; it is worked backward from typical entry age. The gathering pass tagged this attested, which its own note contradicted.
stops.campa: A scholarship carries him out of Lewisham to Eton College, the oldest classroom in England, where most boys arrive already knowing what they will inherit and he arrives knowing arithmetic. No source consulted gives the year he enters. Between chapel and the playing fields he proves himself the sort of mathematician masters remember, and Eton's towers, which have produced prime ministers by the dozen, take no particular notice of a scholarship boy from a bank clerk's family in south London.
suggested_refs: Eton College school lists and King's Scholars registers for the later 1930s

stops.name: Eton College, the Tomline Prize
stops.date_confidence: attested year, month and day unknown; Wikipedia, 'Tony Skyrme', gives 1939 for the Tomline Prize.
stops.campa: In 1939, with Europe tipping into war, Skyrme takes the Tomline Prize, Eton's prize for mathematics. Nothing about the achievement is martial. It is pencil and proof, an argument well made, judged by masters whose own certainties have about eighteen months left to run. He is sixteen. The war that will conscript him before he is twenty-one is still a thing in the newspapers, and the only campaign he is winning is fought over integrals in a room where the curtains will shortly be drawn for other reasons.
suggested_refs: The Eton College prize rolls, Tomline Prize for mathematics, 1939

stops.name: Eton College, the Russell Prize
stops.date_confidence: attested year, month and day unknown; Wikipedia, 'Tony Skyrme', gives 1940 for the Russell Prize.
stops.campa: A year later, with the Battle of Britain fought in the sky above southern England, he takes the Russell Prize as well, and the school goes on teaching under blackout curtains. Two mathematics prizes in two years marks a boy as exceptional even by Eton's inflated standard. The path runs from here to Trinity College, Cambridge, and from Trinity, a great deal faster than anyone at the school could guess, into the interior arithmetic of a nuclear weapon.
suggested_refs: The Eton College prize rolls, Russell Prize, 1940

stops.name: Trinity College, Cambridge, going up to read mathematics
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Wikipedia gives 1940 but not as a matriculation date; it follows from the Russell Prize year. October is the Michaelmas convention, not a documented day. Pin inherited byte-identical from the corpus Trinity College coordinate used in newton.journey.json and niels_bohr.journey.json.
stops.campa: Skyrme goes up to Trinity College, Cambridge, to read mathematics. He takes rooms in a college built centuries before mathematics had anything to do with bombs, on the same staircases where Isaac Newton kept his rooms and ground his own lenses. Around him undergraduates are being called up one by one. The mathematicians are left alone for the moment, and nobody in college explains why, and Skyrme works through proofs in a Cambridge that is quietly reserving him for something.
suggested_refs: Trinity College admissions registers, Michaelmas 1940

stops.name: Trinity College, Cambridge, placed a wrangler
stops.date_confidence: attested year; the Tripos month is conventional, no exact date in sources consulted.
stops.campa: He is placed a wrangler in Part I of the Mathematical Tripos, the ancient Cambridge word for the top rank of the examination, a mark that separates the merely clever from the rest and carries more weight in Cambridge mythology than any medal he will later be given. The war is two years old. Within a year the university's mathematicians, Skyrme among them, will be taken wholesale into Britain's atomic weapons work, their proofs redirected toward the behaviour of plutonium under pressure.
suggested_refs: The Cambridge Mathematical Tripos class lists, Part I, 1942

stops.name: Cambridge, president of the Archimedeans
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and a flagged contradiction. Wikipedia, 'Tony Skyrme', reports the presidency but gives no year; the gathering pass supplied 1942 and tagged it attested. Wikipedia, 'The Archimedeans', does not list Skyrme among past presidents at all. The two are left unreconciled.
stops.campa: He serves as president of the Archimedeans, the Cambridge undergraduate mathematics society, presiding over papers and arguments in a university dimmed for war. The record is loose here in a way worth saying aloud. The article that reports the presidency gives no year for it, and the article on the society itself does not list him among its presidents. Two accounts sit side by side and disagree. Neither is adjudicated here. He presided; when, and whether the society remembers, is open.
suggested_refs: The Archimedeans' own list of past presidents, checked against Kibble's memoir

stops.name: Trinity College, Cambridge, Part III and the starred first
stops.date_confidence: attested year; month conventional. The gathering pass placed Freeman Dyson in this cohort, which is false: Dyson was at RAF Bomber Command from 1943 and took his BA in 1945.
stops.campa: Skyrme completes Part III of the Mathematical Tripos with a starred first, in a Trinity cohort that also holds James Lighthill and Fritz Ursell, names that will each carry weight for fifty years. The degree is barely conferred before the state takes him. Rudolf Peierls, already deep inside the secret work, recruits him as a mathematician that same year. Pure mathematics gives way to the physics of a weapon with almost no transition, and no record survives of him objecting to any part of it.
suggested_refs: The Cambridge Mathematical Tripos class lists, Part III, 1943

segments.name: Under Peierls: Birmingham to the Mesa

stops.name: University of Birmingham, drafted under Rudolf Peierls
stops.date_confidence: year attested, place reconstructed. Wikipedia states only that Skyrme was drafted as a mathematician under Peierls in 1943 and names no city; Birmingham is inference from Peierls's chair there. The gathering pass tagged the place attested, which it is not.
stops.campa: Skyrme is drafted into war work as a mathematician under Rudolf Peierls, who leads the team on the theoretical side of atomic energy. The source names Peierls and names no city. Birmingham is inference: Peierls has held the chair in applied mathematics here since 1937, and the theoretical work of Tube Alloys, authorised in August 1941, runs out of his department. The city is under bombardment. Inside one building a small group of men is deciding what a chain reaction requires.
suggested_refs: Tube Alloys theoretical files, Birmingham 1941-1943; Peierls's own correspondence

stops.name: Columbia University, the diffusion cascade at the SAM Laboratories
stops.date_confidence: attested month and year; 'British Mission to the Manhattan Project' gives March 1944 for his arrival in New York. Day unknown.
stops.campa: Skyrme arrives in New York and joins the work of the Kellex Corporation and Harold Urey's Substitute Alloy Materials laboratories at Columbia, on the design of the gaseous diffusion plant that will separate uranium-235 from its heavier twin. Klaus Fuchs is still in the building; he leaves for New Mexico in August, passing everything he knows to Moscow as he goes. Skyrme's problem is the cascade itself, the plumbing of the bomb rather than its detonation. Four months, and he is moved again.
suggested_refs: British Mission personnel lists, SAM Laboratories and Kellex, spring 1944
sources: Wikipedia, 'British Mission to the Manhattan Project'

stops.name: Los Alamos, the British Mission arrives on the mesa
stops.date_confidence: attested month and year; day unknown. Pin inherited byte-identical from the corpus Los Alamos coordinate used in robert_oppenheimer, richard_feynman, von_neumann, fermi and niels_bohr journey files.
stops.campa: He follows Peierls to Los Alamos, onto a fenced mesa of pine at seven thousand feet that appears on no map sold to the public. Robert Oppenheimer runs the site. Niels Bohr has already passed through, arriving the previous December under the name Nicholas Baker; Richard Feynman is in Bethe's theoretical division; John von Neumann is working the geometry of the implosion lenses. Skyrme joins the British Mission, one more young mathematician inside the largest arithmetic problem ever set.
suggested_refs: British Mission roster at Los Alamos, July 1944
sources: Wikipedia, 'British Mission to the Manhattan Project'

stops.name: Los Alamos, the punched cards and the implosion
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction of the date only. The implosion work and the punched-card machines are attested for Skyrme's Los Alamos period; December 1944 is a placeholder inside that period, not a documented month.
stops.campa: The plutonium implosion problem is a question about symmetry: how to crush a sphere inward evenly enough that it reaches critical mass rather than blowing itself apart. Skyrme works it on IBM punched-card tabulating machines, in the same rooms of clattering hardware Feynman organises into a computing line, and Enrico Fermi arrives in September to head F Division on the same mesa. On the sixteenth of July 1945 the answer is tested at a site called Trinity. Whether Skyrme is there, no source consulted says.
suggested_refs: The Los Alamos IBM punched-card computing group records, 1944-1945
sources: Wikipedia, 'British Mission to the Manhattan Project'

stops.name: Oxford, the Clarendon Laboratory as a stand-in
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction throughout. No source consulted dates the Oxford fellowship, names the college, or names the department; the Clarendon Laboratory is a substituted landmark, declared as such. The gathering pass gave '1945/46' and tagged it attested.
stops.campa: A fellowship at Oxford follows the war, his first post as a civilian rather than a conscript. Almost nothing about it is documented. No source consulted gives the year, names the college, or names the department, and the Clarendon Laboratory stands here only as a physics landmark, not as a place he is known to have worked. Wikipedia mentions Oxford and stops there. He is twenty-three, a veteran of Los Alamos, and fifteen years from the field theory that will carry his name.
suggested_refs: Oxford college fellowship records, 1945-1947; Kibble's memoir would settle this

stops.name: University of Birmingham, research fellow in the rebuilt department
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No source consulted dates the Birmingham fellowship; the gathering pass supplied 1947 without support. Peierls's return to England in January 1946 is attested and fixes the earliest plausible date.
stops.campa: Skyrme takes a research fellowship at Birmingham, returning to the department where his war began. Peierls has come back to England in January 1946 and is rebuilding the place into one of the strongest centres for theoretical physics in the country. The work is unclassified now. Skyrme starts on the slower problem of how nucleons behave at short range, groundwork that will not come to anything for a decade. No source dates the fellowship, and the year given here is a reconstruction.
suggested_refs: University of Birmingham department of mathematical physics staff records, 1946-1948

stops.name: Saas-Fee, the skiing photographs
stops.date_confidence: attested month and year; day unknown. One of the very few precisely dated private facts in the life.
stops.campa: In April Skyrme goes skiing at Saas-Fee, high in the Valais, and the photographs survive: snow, peaks, a young physicist off the leash of Birmingham and the nucleus. It is one of the very few precisely dated private facts in the whole life, and it survives because he is a serious amateur photographer who keeps his negatives. The man on the slope spent a year of his twenties calculating how to compress plutonium into a smaller sphere. The negatives end up in the Bodleian.
suggested_refs: The Skyrme photograph collection, Bodleian Libraries: the Saas-Fee series, April 1947

stops.name: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, a year on the circuit
stops.date_confidence: attested academic year 1948-1949; the September start is the conventional term date, not a documented one.
stops.campa: The academic year takes Skyrme to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, one stop on the transatlantic postdoctoral circuit that the brightest theorists of his generation all ride. Cambridge, Massachusetts, is thick with returning war scientists publishing work that secrecy had held back for five years. What Skyrme himself does at MIT is not recorded in any source consulted. Only the trajectory is legible: Oxford, Birmingham, here, Princeton, and then home to one place for twelve years.
suggested_refs: MIT physics department visitor and research-associate records, 1948-1949

stops.name: Birmingham, the marriage to Dorothy Millest
stops.date_confidence: year attested, place reconstructed. No source consulted names a venue, a town, or a country for the wedding; 1949 straddles his Birmingham base and his American year. Birmingham is a reconstruction from the couple's professional base.
stops.campa: Skyrme marries Dorothy Mildred Millest, a lecturer in experimental nuclear physics. No source consulted names a venue, a town, or even a country for the wedding, and the year straddles his Birmingham base and his American one; the pin is a reconstruction, placed where the couple are professionally rooted. Within a year Dorothy holds her own post at Harwell beside him. There are no children, and the marriage lasts the rest of his life, another thirty-eight years.
suggested_refs: English marriage registers for 1949, and Kibble's memoir for the venue

stops.name: Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton, a member for the year
stops.date_confidence: attested academic year 1949-1950; September is the conventional term start. Coordinate taken from the afterlife lens value, essentially exact against Nominatim's 40.3323, -74.6658; the geography lens's 40.3292, -74.665 is discarded.
stops.campa: From MIT he moves to the Institute for Advanced Study for the year, into Fuld Hall, where Albert Einstein still walks the grounds and Oppenheimer, four years off the mesa, is now director. It is the summit of the postwar circuit and Skyrme reaches it before he is thirty, on wartime arithmetic and a Cambridge starred first. What he works on there is not recorded anywhere consulted. He goes home to Britain afterward, and the ideas that outlast him wait until he does.
suggested_refs: Institute for Advanced Study membership lists, School of Mathematics, 1949-1950
sources: Nominatim, coordinate check on the Institute for Advanced Study

stops.name: Harwell, two physicists at one establishment
stops.date_confidence: attested year, month and day unknown; Wikipedia gives 1950 to 1962 for both Skyrme and Dorothy at Harwell. Coordinate corrected from the gathering pass's 51.571, -1.317, about 1.1 km south-west of the site; Nominatim gives 51.5795, -1.3082 for Harwell Campus.
stops.campa: Skyrme and Dorothy both take posts at the Atomic Energy Research Establishment at Harwell, Britain's central nuclear site, laid out on a former Royal Air Force station under the Berkshire Downs. Two physicists married to each other and employed at the same establishment is an unusual arrangement for 1950, and nobody in the record appears to have made an issue of it. Harwell holds them twelve years, the longest fixed posting of his life, and the circuit of fellowships that carried him through his twenties ends here.
suggested_refs: AERE Harwell staff registers, 1950-1962
sources: Nominatim, coordinate check on Harwell Campus

stops.name: Harwell, head of the theoretical nuclear physics group
stops.date_confidence: attested year, month and day unknown.
stops.campa: By 1954 Skyrme heads the theoretical nuclear physics group, directing a team that includes the young John Bell, whose own inequality will reorder the argument about quantum mechanics a decade later. Harwell in the fifties is a walled campus of reactors and offices where a country's nuclear ambitions are worked out on blackboards. Skyrme runs the group with the rigour that took Eton's two prizes fifteen years earlier, the subject now the nucleus rather than the bomb that splits it.
suggested_refs: AERE theoretical physics division reports, 1954-1962

stops.name: Harwell, the three-body method and the Skyrme force
stops.date_confidence: undated. No source consulted dates the three-body short-range method; it belongs somewhere in the Harwell years and 1955 is a placeholder inside that span.
stops.campa: He develops a method for handling short-range forces in three-body nuclear problems, machinery far less famous than the skyrmion and useful to working physicists for decades after. No source consulted dates it. It belongs to the Harwell years and nothing narrower can honestly be said. The work is unglamorous and undated, and it keeps a field running while its author drifts toward a problem nobody has set him. The zero-range potential of these same years is still called the Skyrme force.
suggested_refs: The Skyrme force in modern nuclear structure codes; the original three-body treatment

stops.name: Dover, the symbolic threshold
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The 1958-1959 circumnavigation is attested; Dover is a symbolic departure point, not a documented waypoint, and no month is recorded. The gathering pass's 'thirteen months later' is invented precision: the source says one year.
stops.campa: Skyrme and Dorothy set out from Britain on a one-year overland circumnavigation of the globe by car and Land Rover, tourists rather than physicists for the length of it. No route survives. Not a border crossing, not a campsite, not one waypoint is named in any source consulted, and Dover stands here as a symbolic threshold only, the last English coastline before the continent takes the tracks. What is documented is the departure, the year, and what the year does to the two of them.
suggested_refs: The Skyrme photograph collection, Bodleian Libraries: the 1958-1959 circumnavigation series

stops.name: Lake Gardens, Kuala Lumpur, the gardens that decide it
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The source records only that on the 1958-1959 tour they fell in love with the tropical gardens of Malaysia and decided to settle there; no garden is named and no date is given. Lake Gardens is a substituted landmark, declared as such.
stops.campa: Somewhere on the circuit they pass through Malaya and fall in love with the tropical gardens, which is the whole of the recorded motive and is worth stating plainly because it is so much smaller than the consequence. No garden is named in the source. Kuala Lumpur's Lake Gardens, laid out under colonial administration decades earlier, stands in as the likeliest thing a touring couple walked through in 1958. From this follows the decision to leave Harwell for the other side of the world.
suggested_refs: The Perdana Botanical Garden, laid out from 1888 under the colonial administration

stops.name: Harwell, the effective nuclear potential
stops.date_confidence: attested year, month and day unknown. Corrected from the gathering pass's 1958: Wikipedia's own citation reads Skyrme, T.H.R. (1959), 'The effective nuclear potential', Nuclear Physics 9 (4): 615-634.
stops.campa: Skyrme publishes 'The effective nuclear potential' in Nuclear Physics, volume nine, pages six hundred and fifteen to six hundred and thirty-four. It is the zero-range force that nuclear structure calculations will still be running on sixty years later, and it is the last thoroughly conventional thing he writes. His name attaches to it as a tool rather than as an idea. What comes next is not a tool, and for eighteen years almost nobody in physics will know what to do with it.
suggested_refs: T.H.R. Skyrme, 'The effective nuclear potential', Nuclear Physics 9 (4): 615-634 (1959)

stops.name: Harwell, A Non-Linear Field Theory
stops.date_confidence: attested; Proc. Roy. Soc. Lond. A 260, 127-138, February 1961. The day is taken from the afterlife lens and is the publication date given there.
stops.campa: The Proceedings of the Royal Society publishes 'A Non-Linear Field Theory,' written at Harwell. Skyrme proposes that a nucleon is not a point but a knot: a stable topological twist in a continuous field, holding its shape because the geometry of the field will not let it come undone. It is an unfashionable idea in 1961, closer to Kelvin's vortex atoms than to the particle physics of the day. Eighteen years pass before the discipline has the vocabulary to see what he has put on the page.
stops.quote: The periodicity in these variables means that they are not uniquely determined (in the classical sense) by the physical state of the system. In regions of weak field the different determinations of angle generate a set of equivalent descriptions, forming separate sheets of a multiple-valued system; but when the fields become strong these sheets may cross one another, forming singularities.
stops.quote_source: T.H.R. Skyrme, 'A Non-Linear Field Theory,' Proc. Roy. Soc. Lond. A 260, 127-138 (1961), quoted in Ian J.R. Aitchison, 'Tony Skyrme and the Origins of Skyrmions,' arXiv:2001.09944 (2020), p.8
suggested_refs: T.H.R. Skyrme, 'A Non-Linear Field Theory', Proc. Roy. Soc. A 260: 127-138 (1961)
sources: Ian J.R. Aitchison, arXiv:2001.09944, p.8 (read as PDF)

stops.name: Harwell, A Unified Field Theory of Mesons and Baryons
stops.date_confidence: attested year, month and day unknown; Nucl. Phys. 31, 556-569 (1962).
stops.campa: 'A Unified Field Theory of Mesons and Baryons' follows in Nuclear Physics, the last paper of the Harwell years and the one that carries the soliton model of the nucleon furthest. He shows how a non-linear meson field can contain its own sources, and how those sources may be idealised down to points in the manner of the conventional theories. He is about to leave the establishment entirely. The paper sits largely unread while he goes, and keeps sitting unread for most of two decades.
stops.quote: Some aspects of a field theory, similar to but more realistic than, that examined in the preceding paper are discussed. The way in which a non-linear meson field theory of this type may contain its own sources, and how these may be idealised to point singularities, as in the conventional field theories of interacting linear systems, is formulated. The structure of the particle source in the classical theory is calculated, and some qualitative features of the interactions between these particles and mesons are described.
stops.quote_source: T.H.R. Skyrme, 'A Unified Field Theory of Mesons and Baryons,' Nucl. Phys. 31, 556-569 (1962), published abstract, via the INSPIRE-HEP literature record (Elsevier)
suggested_refs: T.H.R. Skyrme, 'A Unified Field Theory of Mesons and Baryons', Nucl. Phys. 31: 556-569 (1962)

stops.name: University of Malaya, the professorship taken for a garden
stops.date_confidence: attested year; September is the conventional academic start, not a documented date. Two gathering-pass errors removed here: Malaya became independent on 31 August 1957, so 1962 is five years past independence and not eight, and the Dewan Tunku Canselor did not yet exist on the campus.
stops.campa: Skyrme leaves Harwell after twelve years for a professorship at the University of Malaya in Kuala Lumpur, acting on a decision made four years earlier in a garden. The country is five years past independence from British rule and the university is young. The recorded reason for the move is the gardens, and no source consulted offers another motive. He goes from Britain's premier atomic site to a tropical campus because he and his wife liked the place.
suggested_refs: University of Malaya calendars and staff lists, 1962-1964
sources: Nominatim, coordinate check on Universiti Malaya

stops.name: University of Malaya, two contented years
stops.date_confidence: attested span 1962-1964; month and day of departure unknown.
stops.campa: Two years in Kuala Lumpur, the only stretch of his working life spent wholly outside Britain, Europe, and America, and by the surviving accounts a contented one. He teaches mathematical physics to students on the near side of a colonial rupture recently closed. The soliton paper published just before he left sits unnoticed in the literature throughout, cited by almost nobody. Recognition is another fifteen years off. In 1964 he goes back to Britain and does not leave it again.
suggested_refs: University of Malaya physics teaching records, 1962-1964

stops.name: University of Birmingham, Professor of Mathematical Physics
stops.date_confidence: attested year; October is the conventional academic start. Coordinate is the confirmed Edgbaston campus point; the gathering pass's Watson Building value 52.4498, -1.9309 could not be verified against Nominatim and is not used.
stops.campa: Skyrme is appointed Professor of Mathematical Physics at the University of Birmingham, the department he has now entered three times: as a wartime conscript, as a postwar fellow, and now as its senior mathematical physicist. Peierls is not there to meet him. Peierls left for the Wykeham chair at Oxford the year before, so Skyrme inherits the department rather than rejoining his patron. He holds the chair twenty-three years, until he dies, longer than any other posting of his career.
suggested_refs: University of Birmingham calendars, chair of mathematical physics, 1964-1987

stops.name: Birmingham, Kinks and the Dirac Equation
stops.date_confidence: attested year, month and day unknown; J. Math. Phys. 12, 1735-1743 (1971).
stops.campa: 'Kinks and the Dirac Equation' appears in the Journal of Mathematical Physics, Skyrme still working the same vein a decade on, still describing particle-like structures in a meson field and showing how collective coordinates recover the Dirac equation from them. Almost nobody follows. The Birmingham years are quiet: lectures, students, a chair held steadily while the model he built at Harwell waits in the literature for a generation of physicists who have not yet arrived to read it.
stops.quote: In a model quantum theory of interacting mesons, the motion of certain conserved particlelike structures is discussed. It is shown how collective coordinates may be introduced to describe them, leading, in lowest approximation, to a Dirac equation.
stops.quote_source: T.H.R. Skyrme, 'Kinks and the Dirac Equation,' J. Math. Phys. 12, 1735-1743 (1971), published abstract, via the INSPIRE-HEP literature record
suggested_refs: T.H.R. Skyrme, 'Kinks and the Dirac Equation', J. Math. Phys. 12: 1735-1743 (1971)

stops.name: Birmingham, the word skyrmion enters the literature
stops.date_confidence: attested year, month and day unknown. Corrected from the gathering pass's 1982, which contradicted its own other entries: Wikipedia, 'Skyrmion', gives 1979, Pak and Tze, 'Chiral solitons and current algebra', Annals of Physics 117 (1): 164-194. The downstream figures change with it, from twenty-one years to eighteen and from age fifty-nine to fifty-six.
stops.campa: The word skyrmion enters the physics literature, coined not by Skyrme but by Pak and Tze in 'Chiral solitons and current algebra' in the Annals of Physics. Eighteen years have passed since the original paper. He is fifty-six, still teaching at Birmingham, and lives to watch his own surname become a common noun in a literature that had left the paper alone for most of two decades. The thing named is a shape. It is the only monument he will ever get.
suggested_refs: N.K. Pak and H.C. Tze, 'Chiral solitons and current algebra', Annals of Physics 117 (1): 164-194 (1979)

stops.name: Princeton, the model revived by Adkins, Nappi and Witten
stops.date_confidence: attested year, month and day unknown. The pin is the corpus Princeton coordinate and stands for the town: the 1983 paper's institutional address is the university's physics department rather than the Institute for Advanced Study.
stops.campa: Gregory Adkins, Chiara Nappi, and Edward Witten apply the Skyrme model quantitatively to the properties of the nucleon and get them right to roughly thirty percent, from a model built in 1961 out of pure geometry. Quantum chromodynamics has by now supplied the vocabulary Skyrme lacked. The pin here is the town rather than a building, since the paper's address is the university and not the Institute. Interest in the model revives, twenty-two years late.
suggested_refs: G.S. Adkins, C.R. Nappi and E. Witten, 'Static properties of nucleons in the Skyrme model' (1983)

stops.name: Cosener's House, Abingdon, the origins told in his own voice
stops.date_confidence: attested year, month and day unknown, and one oddity flagged: the talk is dated 1984 but printed in the volume for Peierls's eightieth birthday, and Peierls turned eighty in 1987. No source consulted explains the gap. The coordinate is Abingdon and is approximate.
stops.campa: At Cosener's House in Abingdon, Skyrme gives a talk on where the skyrmion came from, and traces it back past the field equations to his grandfather's tide-predicting machine and to Lord Kelvin's insistence that understanding a thing means being able to build its mechanism. The talk is reconstructed and printed four years later in the volume for Peierls's eightieth birthday, which is itself odd arithmetic, since Peierls turns eighty in 1987. No source consulted explains the gap.
stops.quote: I can never satisfy myself until I can make a mechanical model of a thing. If I can make a mechanical model all the way through I can understand it. As long as I cannot make a mechanical model all the way through I cannot understand; and that is why I cannot get the electromagnetic theory.

stops.name: The Royal Society, Carlton House Terrace, the Hughes Medal
stops.date_confidence: attested year, month and day unknown. Coordinate corrected from the gathering pass's 51.5014, -0.1419, which fell near Green Park about a kilometre away; Nominatim gives 51.5060, -0.1320 for Carlton House Terrace.
stops.campa: The Royal Society awards Skyrme the Hughes Medal at Carlton House Terrace, the citation naming his discovery that particle-like entities simulating the properties of baryons can occur in non-linear meson field theories. He is sixty-two, two years from death. He is never elected a Fellow of the Society that gives him the medal, an omission the field has never quite explained. The medal is the fullest acknowledgment the Royal Society ever gives him.
suggested_refs: The Royal Society Hughes Medal citation, 1985
sources: Nominatim, coordinate check on Carlton House Terrace

stops.name: Selly Oak Hospital, death after routine surgery
stops.date_confidence: attested. Coordinate corrected: the gathering pass gave two different and both wrong values for the same building, 52.4327, -1.9385 and 52.4344, -1.9484. Wikipedia, 'Selly Oak Hospital', gives 52 deg 26 min 13.31 sec N, 1 deg 56 min 13.60 sec W.
stops.campa: Skyrme dies at Selly Oak Hospital in Birmingham of an embolism following what the record calls routine surgery. He is sixty-four and still holds the chair. Dorothy survives him; there are no children. The obituary notices measure him as a competent Harwell nuclear theorist who had one odd idea, and the fuller reckoning, in which the odd idea turns out to describe both baryons and magnetic matter, accumulates through the decades after, when he is not there to read any of it.
suggested_refs: T.W.B. Kibble, 'Tony Hilton Royle Skyrme', Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society (1988), doi 10.1098/rsbm.1988.0022, paywalled and unread here

stops.name: Bodleian Libraries, Oxford, the photographs
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction of the date. The deposit of the photograph collection is attested; no source consulted gives the year it arrived, and 1988 is a placeholder for the period after his death.
stops.campa: His photograph collection comes to rest at the Bodleian Libraries in Oxford, the university where his own postwar fellowship began and where almost nothing else about him is documented. He photographed all his life: the Alps in 1947, a year of overland road across four continents. The archive is the closest thing to a travel diary the record holds for a man whose itineraries are otherwise reconstructed at second hand. No source consulted gives the year the collection arrived.
suggested_refs: The Skyrme photograph collection, Bodleian Libraries, Oxford

stops.campa: No source consulted records a grave or a burial plot. Whether Skyrme was buried or cremated, and where, is not in the reachable English-language record; no obituary or grave registry answered the question in this search. Nor is there a plaque, a monument, a named building, or a centenary event. The Royal Society memoir that would settle most of it sits behind a paywall. Lewisham, where he was born, has nothing on any wall, and this stop is the gap itself.

stops.campa: World Scientific publishes Selected Papers, with Commentary, of Tony Hilton Royle Skyrme, edited by Gerald Brown, as volume three of its series in twentieth-century physics. It is the first substantial editorial treatment of the collected work, seven years after the author's death. The pin is the publisher's city, not a place Skyrme ever worked. No Spanish edition or other translation could be confirmed. The commentary is the argument, made at last in one place, that the odd 1961 paper was never a curiosity.

stops.name: Birmingham, the skyrmion found in matter
stops.date_confidence: attested year for the atomic-scale observation, month and day unknown; the room-temperature lattices follow around 2015. The pin is not the laboratory: no source consulted names where the experiments were done, so Birmingham stands for the man rather than the work.
stops.campa: An atomic-scale skyrmion lattice is observed in an iron monolayer on iridium, and within a few years room-temperature Bloch skyrmion lattices follow in cobalt and palladium multilayers, candidates for storing data as knots in a magnetic film. The mathematics is his, transplanted out of the nucleus into condensed matter. No source consulted names the laboratories, so the pin stands for the man and not the experiment: Birmingham, where the chair was, where nothing is marked.
suggested_refs: The 2011 atomic-scale magnetic skyrmion lattice in Fe/Ir(111); room-temperature Co/Pd skyrmion lattices, c. 2015
